title: Review: The Time Value of Money
subtitle: PV, FV, NPV, IRR, WACC - connecting the whole Time Value of Money track
openingQuestion: If you only remember one principle from this track, what is it?
openingOptions: A dollar today is always worth more than a dollar in the future, because of opportunity cost and risk
A higher interest rate is good
explanation: This whole track is built on a single idea: money has a price over time, so two amounts at two different points in time can't be compared directly. From that comes present value and future value; applied to a project's cash flow it becomes NPV and IRR; applied to a whole company's cash flow it becomes the discounted cash flow model, with the discount rate being exactly the weighted average cost of capital. Nothing above stands independently of that original idea.

diagram.label: Money today can earn a return, so it's worth more than money next year
From that comes present value and future value
Applied to project cash flow, it becomes NPV and IRR
Applied to an entire company, it becomes DCF, discounted by WACC

realWorldExample.company: A summary of financial valuation tools
realWorldExample.description: From basic PV/FV to NPV, IRR, WACC - this toolkit is used every day by every CFO, financial analyst, and investment bank in the world to make decisions on trillions of dollars of investment each year, from opening a small branch to enormous M&A deals.

quiz.question: Why does Terminal Value account for 60-80% of total DCF value?
options: Because it packages the entire cash flow from after the forecast period out to infinity
Because the cash flow in the final years is always larger than the early years
Because it isn't discounted the way the detailed forecast is
Because valuation standards mandate a minimum weight for this component
quiz.explanation: A DCF forecasts in detail for 5-10 years, but the business keeps operating forever. Terminal Value = PV of all cash flow from year n+1 onward = large → accounts for 60-80% of total value. The growth assumption g is highly sensitive.

quiz.question: After finishing the Time Value of Money track, what is the most important skill to carry forward into the Corporate Finance track?
options: Memorizing the WACC formula and standard annuity factors by heart
Reducing every decision to a present value so it can be compared
Knowing how to use a financial calculator to punch through problems quickly
Remembering the minimum IRR threshold businesses typically require
quiz.explanation: The Time Value of Money track builds the 'common language' of quantitative finance: PV, NPV, WACC aren't separate formulas but the SAME way of thinking - reducing every decision to a comparable present value. The entire Corporate Finance track and the Stock Valuation track build directly on this way of thinking.

quiz.question: How are PV, NPV, IRR, and WACC related to each other?
options: WACC is calculated from IRR, while NPV is calculated from the PV of capital invested
Four independent metrics, used for four different types of decisions
NPV uses WACC to discount; IRR is the r that makes NPV equal to zero
IRR and NPV always give the same ranking when comparing projects
quiz.explanation: All of them are the same discounting operation viewed from different angles: PV is the brick, NPV stacks them up and subtracts the outlay, WACC is the rate used to discount, IRR is the rate that makes that total equal zero.

quiz.question: Among the four project appraisal criteria, which is most trustworthy when you must pick one?
options: Discounted Payback, because it both discounts and measures time
IRR, because a percentage is easy to compare across projects
Payback, because it most clearly reflects liquidity risk
NPV, because it directly measures the absolute value created
quiz.explanation: NPV correctly answers the question a business needs: how much additional value does this project create. IRR ignores scale, Payback ignores everything after the payback point - both are supplementary indicators, not the primary criterion.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental reason a dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year?
options: Because it can be invested to earn a return starting today
Because inflation will certainly erode its value next year
Because the risk of not receiving the money increases over time
Because central banks always keep interest rates positive
quiz.explanation: Inflation and risk are two additional reasons, but the root cause is opportunity cost: money today can start working immediately. Even with zero inflation and zero risk, a dollar today is still worth more.

keyTakeaways: TVM: 1 dollar today > 1 dollar in the future
NPV = the best criterion for investment decisions
WACC = the discount rate, DCF = valuation by discounted cash flow

practicePrompt.question: After reviewing the Time Value of Money track, you've concluded that PV, FV, discounting, compounding, annuities, perpetuities, NPV, and IRR all revolve around a single core principle. What is that principle?
options: TVM: 1 dollar today > 1 dollar in the future - because money today can be invested to earn a return, and every formula in this track (PV, FV, NPV, IRR...) is a different application of this same core principle
Each formula in this track is independent with no common relationship between them
The core principle is that interest rates are always fixed and never change in any financial situation
TVM only applies to corporate investment decisions, not to personal finance
practicePrompt.explanation: TVM (Time Value of Money): 1 dollar today > 1 dollar in the future - this is the core principle running through the entire track: PV/FV is how you convert money across time points, NPV/IRR apply this principle to evaluate investment projects, annuities/perpetuities are special cash flow shapes that need to be discounted correctly.

summary.keyIdea: TVM: 1 dollar today > 1 dollar in the future
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: NPV = the best criterion for investment decisions

sections.text: The Time Value of Money track revolves around a single idea, repeated in many forms: money has value over time, and every serious financial decision comes down to comparing the present value of cash flows, discounted at the appropriate level of risk.
A map of the formulas covered

PV = FV/(1+r)^n - pulls future money back to today. FV = PV×(1+r)^n - pushes today's money into the future through compounding. PV Annuity = PMT×[(1−(1+r)^−n)/r] - values a level cash flow with a fixed term. PV Perpetuity = C/r (or C/(r−g) with growth) - values a cash flow that lasts forever. NPV = PV(cash flow) − Initial investment - the investment decision criterion. IRR - the discount rate that makes NPV=0. WACC = Ke×(E/V) + Kd×(1−T)×(D/V) - the weighted average cost of capital, used as the standard discount rate in DCF.
Why Terminal Value accounts for most of a DCF's value

A DCF model usually forecasts in detail for only 5-10 years, but a business is assumed to keep operating indefinitely after that. Terminal Value (calculated with the Gordon Growth Model, PV = C/(r−g)) represents the entire value from the last forecast year onward - and because this is the sum of an infinite cash flow, it usually accounts for 60-80% of the total DCF value. This is also why the long-run growth assumption g is the most sensitive and most debated variable in any valuation model.

items: PV/FV: the foundation - one dollar today differs in value from one dollar in the future
Annuity/Perpetuity: special cash flow shapes, each with its own valuation formula
NPV/IRR/Payback: three project appraisal criteria, with NPV the most reliable
Cost of Debt/Cost of Equity/WACC/CAPM/Beta: the toolkit for correctly calculating the discount rate for each type of capital and risk

lines: The entire Corporate Finance track and the Stock Valuation track will continue building directly on the PV/NPV/WACC foundation just covered here.

If you remember just one thing from the Time Value of Money track: every financial decision can be reduced to the question 'what is the present value of this cash flow, once correctly discounted for its risk'.
